records.description: Mossbauer transmission spectra record gamma attenuation as relative source/absorber velocity is varied. A fitted center shift, quadrupole splitting, linewidth and relative spectral area are inferred spectral parameters, distinct from a directly observed atomic geometry, absolute recoilless fraction or complete vibrational density of states. The alpha-induced carbon-neutron component was not included in the earlier publication and changes its background estimate. The fast-neutron value below 0.89 events is an upper bound entering uncertainty, not an additional central count. studies.correctionCheck: Read selected preparation and Stark passages in the published Science 322(5899),231-235 primary paper; visually checked published page 234/Figure 6 and surrounding text in the six-page author-hosted file (one cover plus five article pages). The primary thesis correction is separately cited; the 2008 value remains a historical result. No raw spectra, full covariance, independent electric-field calibration, new Stark fit or collective many-body experiment was reproduced. Crossref metadata shows no update-to record and an empty relation object; the actual author-thesis correction is retained rather than inferring no correction.
studies.finding: The selected KRb singlet v=0 N=0 resonance shifts downward with applied dc field, while the N=2 response splits by angular-momentum projection. The zero-field N=0/N=2 interval is reported as 6.6836(5) GHz. These are spectroscopic frequency differences, before identifying a body-fixed moment through a rotational model. Ni et al. report B_Hz=1.1139(1) GHz and a body-fixed permanent-moment magnitude 0.566(17) D for 40K87Rb X1Sigma+ v=0, inferred from the N=0 Stark curve. The author thesis corrects the moment to 0.574(17) D after a plate-separation error. Use 1 D approximately 3.336e-30 C m. The N=2 curves test consistency within the same experiment.
limitations: The source preparation supplies molecules; the Stark response is not a universal molecular formation pathway or a bulk dielectric experiment.
The initial-state Stark contribution is neglected because the weakly bound starting molecules have a negligible moment in this treatment.
No direct charge-density image, force measurement, independently calibrated electric field or local spectral refit is supplied.

The result uncertainty is dominated by field calibration, not the statistical uncertainty of an isolated spectral line. Thesis Section 8.3 states 3%, while apparatus Section 3.2 estimates 3-5% and lacks independent field calibration; no reconciled error is invented.
The body-fixed moment does not imply a nonzero laboratory vector average at zero dc field. The thesis correction is not a new dataset or independent confirmation.
The positive dipole values are magnitudes. This selected rotational Stark fit does not determine a signed molecular charge-density map or which atomic end carries the negative charge.

Scan the external dc field over the reported approximately 0-2 kV/cm range using transparent plates outside a glass cell, and record resonance shifts relative to zero field. Rotational-state comparisons supply the rotational constant used in the singlet fit.

studies.correctionCheck: Read published scientific main text and Methods on pages 1-8 of the nine-page primary PDF; visually checked pages 4 and 6, Figures 3 and 5 and Equation 6. Source interpretation uses a non-resonant polarizability interaction; the measured observable is electron diffraction, not an electronic dipole value or a dielectric-constant measurement. No raw image replay, TDSE integration, intensity-profile correction or numerical polarizability extraction was performed. studies.finding: The nitrogen diffraction patterns change with pump-probe delay and show rotational revivals. The reported anisotropy is a ratio of counts in horizontal and vertical angular cones, sampled in 100 fs delay steps with two minutes of accumulation per point. A response near the half revival changes between prolate and oblate angular distributions over about 300 fs. The image-derived alignment moments are reported as <cos^2(theta)>=0.41 for the prolate and 0.28 for the oblate distribution. The common fit gives 100 fs RMS temporal resolution and overlap factor 0.42; its angular simulations agree after time averaging. These state- and pulse-specific results support a polarizability-mediated alignment interpretation, without determining an absolute alpha tensor, net vector orientation or bulk dielectric constant.
limitations: Backing pressure is not molecular sample density or rotational temperature. The pulse is treated as non-resonant in the source model; no perfectly ionization-free preparation is asserted.
The experiment is an axis-alignment response of supplied neutral molecules; it does not require hydrogen bonds or prior ionic charge transfer.

Patterns are four-quadrant symmetrized. The stated anisotropy range 3-4.5 inverse Angstrom partly intersects the missing region below 3.5 inverse Angstrom, which the source extrapolates smoothly to zero.
Diffraction anisotropy is not a directly measured permanent or induced electronic dipole magnitude.
The 0.42 overlap parameter is fitted to this preparation, not a universal aligned fraction, carrier minimum, cooperative threshold or independent validation dataset.
A second angular moment can be anisotropic while the first vector moment is zero; this is not evidence of a permanent nitrogen dipole or collective polar phase.

The source reports 0.7 bar nozzle backing pressure, approximately 6e-5 torr chamber pressure and an alignment-pulse peak intensity 5e13 W/cm^2, at which very faint plasma remains observable.

studies.finding: The selected dried Fe-gluconate specimen has a broad XRD pattern classified as amorphous, in contrast with the crystalline hydrated parent specimen. Fe-57 velocity-dependent transmission spectra show resonant attenuation at finite absorber temperatures across the reported 78-295 K study; Figure 2 displays 78 K and 268 K examples. This is a positive bound-solid Mossbauer case whose absorber is not reported to possess perfect periodic crystal order. The three-doublet analysis yields finite widths and distinct center shifts and quadrupole splittings under the stated spectral model. At 295 K its normalized area quantities a1,a2,a3 are 0.49,0.46,0.52 relative to 78 K. The model-derived effective Debye temperatures differ: Table 2 reports 377(9) K from CS1 and 204(4) K from a1. These results illustrate finite-temperature spectral and vibrational sensitivity, with fitted hyperfine/electronic-environment interpretation, rather than a natural-width measurement or absolute recoilless probability.
limitations: This is one primary experiment context containing sample X-ray characterization and finite-temperature transmission spectroscopy. Its spectra, fitted components, relative areas and Debye interpretations share the same specimen/measurements; they are not independent replications.

The measured sample is powdered Fe-gluconate prepared by dissolution and drying at 50 degrees C. XRD-amorphous is the reported finite-sensitivity diffraction classification, not proof that every atomic neighborhood has no order.

The source reports about 10 mg Fe per cm^2, 1024 channels, source at room temperature, 78-295 K absorber range and temperature stability within plus/minus 0.1 K. These preparation/control values are not error bars on fitted shifts or proof of the thin-absorber approximation for every material.

The quoted typical Table 1 errors are source estimates, without a reconstructed confidence convention or complete covariance/systematic budget. No raw counts, background, thickness correction, calibration fit or independent uncertainty replay was obtained.

The earlier crystalline comparison study and imported Debye/isomer-shift references are not separately reviewed or admitted as additional studies. The original 1959 paper was not obtained as actual article text; a seven-page anthology contents PDF is not that article.

The XRD classification and transmission profiles establish a finite observed case; they do not measure a universal ordering threshold, a unique local coordination geometry or an exactly absent crystalline volume fraction.
Figure 2 displays 78 K and 268 K examples. The study range reaches 295 K; the plotted higher-temperature example must not be relabelled 295 K.

The fitted D1,D2,D3 curves are model components overlaid on measured spectra. Their existence as a useful decomposition does not alone establish three unique phases, three distinct atom positions or an independent magnetic-ordering measurement.
The transmission scale is relative; no new absolute absorption cross section, absolute gamma-emission probability, natural linewidth or independent f measurement is inferred.

Table 1 center shifts are relative to the Co-57/Rh source at room temperature, not automatically to metallic alpha-Fe. Its shift, splitting and full-width-at-half-maximum entries are in mm/s; the fitted widths are not natural nuclear energy widths.

At 295 K the table lists a1,a2,a3 as 0.49,0.46,0.52 after normalization to unity at 78 K. These are relative normalized spectral-area quantities under the stated approximation, not absolute probabilities f(295 K).

The text writes a_k=(A_k/B)/a_k(78 K), with B the background counts. This notation reuses a_k on the normalization reference; retain the stated background and 78 K normalization without claiming a new independent absolute normalization or repaired raw-data definition.

Three-doublet fitting associates D1,D2 with Fe(II) and D3 with Fe(III) from their spectral parameters. Relative component areas are not automatically atom-number fractions when component recoilless fractions differ; no new exact Fe(III) population or unique geometry is admitted.

The source Table 1 nominal area row at 268 K sums to 101.0 percent, so its rounded fitted entries are not promoted to an exact probability-normalized mixture. No correction or recalculated row is invented.

Table 2 gives effective Debye temperatures 377(9) K from CS1 and 204(4) K from a1. Parenthesized errors retain the source convention, without an invented confidence level or full shared-data covariance. The two routes are different weightings/assumptions, not independent proof of one exact Debye temperature.

The page 7 prose refers to Table 3 for these values although the adjacent displayed table is Table 2. This is a source cross-reference discrepancy, not an additional unseen table or a reason to silently renumber the source.
No new Debye integral fit, spectrum decomposition, isotope abundance estimate, magnetic-ordering conclusion, complete phonon spectrum or dynamical lifetime is reproduced.

limitations: PNP detects the ion after coherent radial-to-axial transfer. Its resonant voltages differ for N+ and N2+, changing equilibrium position in stray fields. The SOF protocol keeps the evolution voltage common and changes it only for detection.

The SOF signal is a classical cyclotron amplitude produced by two separated pulses, not a quantum-state amplitude or an entanglement measurement. Figure 1 uses evolution times up to 50 s for the precision estimate.

Figure 2 compares an N+ ion at approximately 5 V with the same species at 10 V and an N2+ ion at 10 V, with a 22.5 mV axial offset. The approximately 3 ppb unequal-voltage shift disappears at the reported precision with the common-voltage procedure.

Table I bounds residual magnetic, electrostatic and relativistic systematic terms at approximately 0.030, 0.025 and 0.020 ppb for the specified N+/N2+ settings. These are configuration-specific error estimates, not zero corrections or universal bounds.

The first two Table II(a) reference ratios depend on electron mass and binding energies. Their agreement near 0.15 ppb tests those controls; it does not prove absence of every systematic effect in all other ion comparisons.
The measured ion has three trap modes. The free cyclotron frequency is reconstructed from their squared frequencies; the trap cyclotron mode alone is not the free frequency.
The paper writes omega_c=q*B/(m*c) in Gaussian units. In SI the expression is omega_c=abs(q)*B/m for the frequency magnitude; an angular frequency differs from cycles per second by 2*pi.

For the same magnetic field, omega_2/omega_1=(m_1/abs(q_1))/(m_2/abs(q_2)). Equal charges permit a mass ratio; the Ar+/Ar++ entry requires the charge factor and is not a literal ratio of almost equal ionic masses.
The ions are loaded and measured alternately, not simultaneously. Removing a fitted magnetic drift does not make all residuals or adjacent ratios statistically independent.
These are reported measurements and conditional inferences. Raw phase records, drift fits, chemical-energy inputs and complete covariance have not been independently replayed.

A charged-ion frequency, neutral-atom mass and inferred neutron mass are different quantities. These results do not establish nucleon formation, lifetime, stability or a universal constituent minimum.

The 1993 and 1994 publications belong to the same MIT measurement program. Disjoint acquisition and cross-publication covariance are not established; the two papers cannot be treated as independent replications or averaged as independent results.
